title: Four years of lessons with Eddie Hudson and what he taught
summary: Randolph studied Goodrich's Analysis of Music with Hudson, passed this on to his pupils, and recalls Hudson's advice about not forming habits you cannot do without.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Yes. So, well, I studied there with

Eddie for about four years. I took harmony, theory of harmony then, Goodrich Analysis of Music -- now, there's where you learn something about music. Then -- and I passed -- I used that with my pupils too. A lot of the information I got out of the books with Eddie Hudson, such things like -- now, you know, we use bars out of context when we say bars. There's a bar line and there's a perpendicular line, see. See, (unintelligible) line runs horizontal and this perpendicular line is the bar line.

Now, that bar line divides the staff in two measures. They rewrite the notes in the measure and if some singer or dancer or even some orchestra leader comes up and they want you to play the last two measures, they'll tell you to play the last two bars. Well, the last two bars maybe sometime on a number is the last two double bars -- the last two bars which isn't anything, and I showed them that, about the last two bars. And such things like, pick up the time. You can't pick --

Yes, you can't -- that's right. You can't pick up that time, you see. And it's things like that I pass on to those -- pass on to them. And quite a few of the little pointers that I got out of Goodrich Analysis of Music, you know, where he takes the music and tears it all to pieces and analyses it. Well, finally, what I want to tell you about Hudson, after this fourth year, I went with Hudson to get my lesson there, and Hudson says to me, he says, 'Well,' he always

called me boy. He said, "Well, boy, four years ago when you came here," he says, "I said to myself, 'This funny looking little juggaboo --'," thats what we usually call one another sometimes, juggaboo, he says, "This funny looking little juggaboo say he's going to do like all the rest of the juggaboos, he's going to take one or two lessons and cut out.'"

He says, "But you didn't -- you kept coming." He says, "I have scratched my head many a day to dig up material for you," that's the average person would say what he said. Well, now (unintelligible) oh, yeah, I'm happy. One of these things, (unintelligible) but when he said that it was ______. A big lump hit me like in the stomach. I looked around in the room and I looked, and it was kind of -- I felt sad because I said to myself, "Now, you won't be coming back here any more."

I always looked forward to coming to Eddie, because Eddie always would sit after a lesson and he would talk me all night about staying out of pool rooms. I'm a married man now, but I'm a young man, see. And tell me, don't allow yourself to get used to something that you can't do without. Such things like that. He told me about a man fished around in an ash tray looking for a cigarette and had to get up at 3:00 o'clock in the morning and got in his car going around to this place to open so he could get a cigarette. He said -- without any -- I don't mean any offense, but he -- just speaking of Eddie Hudson telling me, you know. And so, he was telling me, "Don't allow yourself to get used to something that you just got to have, you just got
to have it." Well, that instilled in me, and I'm that way now, today. He really did wash my brain good.
Yeah. He give me a good brain washing.
And, so, it was sad for me to part from Eddie that way. Well, I went to Kreuger Conservatory for awhile, but I didn't stay therelong because the fact that I got this job playing with the roof garden.
